title: The Space Between the Question and the Answer
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek takes Addy Osmani's guide on keeping your thinking when AI agents do most of your work and translates it for schools. His central point is that the space between asking a question and getting an answer, where thinking used to happen, now lasts seconds, so critical thinking has to be put back deliberately. He describes the slide from delegating a task, to treating the tool's answer as a starting point, to no longer checking it, and cites a Penn study of nearly a thousand high school math students in which an open chatbot hurt exam performance while a hint-giving version did not. He then works through integrity, critical thinking, creativity and discernment, pairing a classroom move for the teacher with a policy move for the school leader in each. Examples include process conferences, predicting before prompting, student-written first drafts, planted-error summaries, and a weekly unplugged block. He concludes that these are old teaching habits that a school now has to rebuild on purpose.
points: Osmani's test for ownership, that you must be able to explain the answer even with the tool's help, gives teachers a simple check for AI over-reliance.
The Penn math study shows the guardrail matters, since an open chatbot raised practice scores but lowered exam scores while a hint-only tutor did no harm.
Having students write their own prediction or thesis before opening the tool gives them something to argue with and helps memory.
Requiring first drafts to come from the student, by hand and in class, protects voice and gives leaders a graded baseline to compare against the final.
Setting the tool to off by default, with a stated purpose on each assignment, teaches that AI use is a decision someone makes for a reason.
quotes: If you want critical thinking in your day, you have to put it there on purpose, because nothing will do it for you by default. And whatever you hand to the machine, the responsibility for the result stays with you.
His test for where you've landed is simple. If you can't explain the answer, even with the tool's help, it isn't yours anymore.

The group given an open chatbot did far better on practice problems and then worse on the closed-laptop exam than students who never had the tool, while a version built to give hints and hold back answers did no harm. The difference was the guardrail.
Walk me through this paragraph. What did the tool suggest that you threw out? It takes three minutes per student and it's the one check a polished artifact can't pass on its own.
Before the tool opens, the student writes her own thesis, her own guess at why the war started. There's good research that the guess itself helps memory, even when it's wrong.
The classroom version is a rule I'd make without apology: first drafts come from the student. By hand, in class, from her own head, before any tool is involved.
Where being wrong is cheap, delegate. Where someone else will live with the consequences, keep the thinking.
A school has to build the space back in on purpose, and a school is the one institution that was always supposed to be doing exactly that.
